model_answer:
Religion 1: Judaism - the Exodus remembered at Passover (Pesach)
The event: Jews remember how God freed their ancestors from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses, around 1250 BCE. After the tenth plague, the angel of death 'passed over' the houses of the Israelites marked with lamb's blood, and the people left Egypt in such a hurry that their bread had no time to rise (Exodus 12).
How it is marked: Passover is an eight-day spring festival. Before it begins, the house is cleaned of all chametz (leavened food). On the first evening families gather for the Seder meal and read the Haggadah, which tells the Exodus story. The youngest child asks the four questions, beginning 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' The foods on the Seder plate each represent part of the story:
- matzah (unleavened bread) - the haste of the escape;
- maror (bitter herbs) - the bitterness of slavery;
- charoset (apple, nut and wine paste) - the mortar used by the slaves in building;
- karpas (a green vegetable) dipped in salt water - the tears of the slaves and new life;
- a roasted shank bone - the Passover lamb;
- a roasted egg - the festival offering and new life.
Four cups of wine are drunk, recalling God's promises of freedom, and a cup is poured for the prophet Elijah, whose return will announce the Messiah. The meal ends with 'Next year in Jerusalem'. Each generation is taught to see itself as if it had personally been freed from Egypt by God.

Religion 2: Christianity - the death and resurrection of Jesus marked at Easter
The event: Christians remember the last days of Jesus' life - the Last Supper, his crucifixion on Good Friday and his resurrection from the dead on the third day.
How it is marked: Easter is the most important Christian festival and follows the forty days of Lent. Holy Week re-enacts the story:
- Palm Sunday recalls Jesus' entry into Jerusalem with the blessing and carrying of palms.
- Holy Thursday recalls the Last Supper, with the Mass of the Lord's Supper and the washing of feet.
- Good Friday recalls the crucifixion: there is no Mass, the Passion is read, and people venerate the cross; many fast.
- At the Easter Vigil on Holy Saturday night, a new fire is lit in the darkness and the Paschal Candle is lit from it, symbolising Christ, the light of the world, rising from death. The Exsultet is sung, the readings tell the story of salvation, water is blessed and new members are baptised, and the 'Alleluia' returns.
- On Easter Sunday Christians celebrate the risen Christ; Easter eggs are a symbol of new life.
Through these rituals Christians not only remember the event but share in it, believing that Christ's victory over death gives them new life.

model_answer:
I will describe the Lord's Prayer (the Our Father) as prayed in the Catholic Church. It is the prayer Jesus himself taught his disciples when they asked, 'Lord, teach us to pray' (Luke 11:1-4; Matthew 6:9-13), and it is prayed at every Mass, in the Rosary and by all Christian denominations.

How religious belief is expressed
- 'Our Father, who art in heaven': Christians believe God is kind and loving like a father. Jesus called God Abba - a child's word like 'Dad' - expressing love and trust. 'Our' shows that all believers are brothers and sisters in one family of God, and 'in heaven' that God is also beyond us.
- 'Hallowed be thy name': belief that God is holy and deserves worship and reverence.
- 'Thy kingdom come, thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven': belief in the Kingdom of God, at the heart of Jesus' preaching, and that people should live by God's will - justice, peace and love - here and now.
- 'Give us this day our daily bread': belief that God provides and that people depend on God for everything; for Catholics it also brings to mind the bread of the Eucharist.
- 'Forgive us our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us': belief in God's mercy, and that those who are forgiven must forgive others.
- 'Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil': belief that God protects and saves people from sin and evil.
At Mass the people add the doxology, 'For the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and for ever', expressing belief that God reigns over all.

model_answer:
I will outline how belief is expressed in Salat (Salah), the ritual prayer of Islam.

What it is
Salat is the second of the Five Pillars of Islam. Muslims pray five times a day - at dawn, midday, afternoon, sunset and night - in the way taught by the Prophet Muhammad. They first perform wudu (ritual washing), face the Ka'ba in Makkah, and pray in Arabic, whatever their nationality. Each unit of prayer (rak'ah) follows set movements: standing, bowing, prostrating with the forehead on the ground, and sitting. Friday midday prayer is said together at the mosque.

How religious belief is expressed
- 'Allahu Akbar' ('God is the greatest'), said at the start and at each change of position, expresses belief that Allah is greater than everything and worthy of all praise.
- The opening chapter of the Qur'an, al-Fatiha, is recited in every rak'ah: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds... Master of the Day of Judgement. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Guide us on the straight path.' This expresses belief in one God (tawhid), in Allah's mercy, in the Day of Judgement and in the need for Allah's guidance.
- Bowing and prostration express belief in submission to Allah - the meaning of the word 'Islam' - and the humility of the believer before the Creator.
- Facing Makkah and praying in Arabic at the same times as Muslims everywhere express belief in the unity of the Umma.
- The prayer ends by sending peace on the Prophet and turning right and left with 'Peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah', expressing belief in Muhammad as the messenger of God and in peace with others.

Name: Leonardo da Vinci.
Leonardo was born in 1452 in Vinci, near Florence in Italy. He trained as an apprentice in the workshop of the artist Verrocchio in Florence.
He worked for rich patrons such as Lorenzo de Medici, the Duke of Milan (Ludovico Sforza) and King Francis I of France. He died in France in 1519.
His most famous painting is the Mona Lisa. He used a new technique called sfumato, where colours blend softly into each other, which makes her smile look mysterious.
He painted The Last Supper on the wall of a monastery in Milan. It uses perspective so that everything leads your eye to Jesus in the centre.
He was also a scientist and inventor. He filled notebooks with designs for a flying machine, a parachute and a tank, written in mirror writing.
He cut up (dissected) dead bodies to study anatomy and made very accurate drawings of the human body, like the Vitruvian Man.
He changed art by making paintings look more realistic and lifelike, and he changed science by showing that you learn by observing and experimenting. He is seen as the perfect "Renaissance man".

marking_scheme:
Six terms explained, 6 x 3 marks, each on a sliding scale out of 3 (3 very good, 2 good/fair, 1 poor, 0 no merit) (18). Only the six highest-scoring answers count.
Accepted meanings: Antisemitism - hostility to or prejudice against Jewish people. Propaganda - organised spreading of information/misinformation to persuade people. Nuremberg Laws - anti-Jewish laws of 1935: Jews no longer German citizens, banned from marrying or having relationships with non-Jews. Gestapo - Nazi secret police who persecuted opponents, including Jews. Kristallnacht - Nazi-organised attack on synagogues, Jewish homes and businesses, November 1938; about 100 killed, thousands arrested. Ghetto - over-crowded, guarded area of a town where Jews were forced to live apart. Concentration camp - place of imprisonment/forced labour/death for those the Nazis saw as enemies. Einsatzgruppen - mobile killing units that followed the German army and murdered Jews and others, often by shooting. Final Solution - the Nazi plan to kill all the Jews of Europe. Genocide - deliberately trying to destroy a group because of religion, nationality, race or ethnicity. Nuremberg Trials - trials of leading Nazis for war crimes and crimes against humanity after WWII. Holocaust denial - antisemitic claims that the Holocaust did not happen or was not serious.
model_answer:
1. Antisemitism: Hatred of, or prejudice against, Jewish people. The Nazis blamed Jews for Germany's problems, like losing World War One.
2. Nuremberg Laws: Laws passed in 1935 that took away Jewish people's German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews.
3. Kristallnacht: "The Night of Broken Glass", 9-10 November 1938, when Nazis attacked Jewish shops, homes and synagogues across Germany. About 100 Jewish people were killed and about 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps.
4. Ghetto: A closed-off part of a city where Jews were forced to live, crowded together with little food, such as the Warsaw Ghetto in Poland.
5. Final Solution: The Nazi plan, agreed at the Wannsee Conference in 1942, to murder all the Jews of Europe, mainly in death camps like Auschwitz.
6. Genocide: The deliberate killing of a whole group of people because of their race, religion or nationality. The Nazis murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust.

(h) In 1971 the Irish Women's Liberation Movement published "Chains or Change", which listed the unfair ways women were treated, and its members appeared on The Late Late Show, so the whole country heard their demands.
They went on the "Contraceptive Train" from Belfast to Dublin in May 1971 to protest against the ban on contraception.
Their campaign helped to end the marriage bar in 1973, so married women could keep working in the civil service.
The Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 gave women equal pay for equal work, and the Employment Equality Act 1977 banned discrimination in jobs.

(c) (i) The theory of Charles Darwin and Alfred Wallace: Living things in a species vary (they are not all the same). More young are produced than can survive, so they compete for food, space and mates. The ones with the most useful characteristics (best adapted) survive and reproduce. This is 'survival of the fittest'. They pass these useful characteristics on to their offspring. Over many generations the species slowly changes.
(ii) Over time, natural selection forms new species (speciation). Different habitats favour different characteristics. Over millions of years, groups of a species living in different places change in different ways until they become new species. So many different species have evolved from common ancestors, which explains the huge variety (diversity) of living things.

model_answer:
Magnesium is in Group 2, so it loses 2 electrons to form Mg²⁺ (valency 2).
Oxygen is in Group 6, so it gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻ (valency 2).

prompt:
1B. Seismic Activity
Explain how the occurrence of earthquakes can be predicted and their effects reduced.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Reference to prediction of earthquakes: 2 marks. Reference to reducing impacts of earthquakes: 2 marks. Explanation: 13 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second reference to prediction and 1 x SRP for a second reference to reducing impacts; all further references must be explained.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Take a broad interpretation of prediction and reducing effects.
- Max 7 x SRPs if only prediction or only reduction of effects is explained.
model_answer:
Predicting earthquakes:
Earthquakes cannot be predicted exactly, but scientists can say where and roughly how likely they are. Most occur along plate boundaries, so mapping fault lines such as the San Andreas Fault in California shows where risk is highest. Seismologists study the history of past earthquakes along a fault; a 'seismic gap', a section that has not moved for a long time, is likely to be building up stress. Seismometers record small tremors (foreshocks), which can come before a big earthquake. Tiltmeters and GPS satellites measure tiny movements and bulging of the ground. Scientists also monitor changes in groundwater levels and the release of radon gas from cracks in the rock. Early warning systems, such as ShakeAlert in the USA and Japan's system, detect the first P-waves and send alerts by phone seconds before the more damaging S-waves arrive, so trains can stop and people can take cover.

Reducing the effects:
Earthquake-proof buildings are the most important way of saving lives, because most deaths are caused by collapsing buildings. In Japan and California, buildings are built with steel frames that bend, deep foundations, and rubber shock absorbers (base isolators) that let the building move separately from the ground. Tall buildings like Taipei 101 have a huge counterweight (tuned mass damper) to reduce swaying. Strict building codes are enforced, and older buildings are retrofitted. Gas and water pipes are made flexible, with automatic shut-off valves, to prevent fires like those after the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. Land-use planning stops building on soft ground that suffers liquefaction. Education is vital: in Japan people practise 'Drop, Cover and Hold On' drills every year on 1 September, and families keep emergency kits. Emergency services plan rescue and medical responses in advance.

In poorer countries such as Haiti (2010), poorly built concrete buildings collapsed and over 200,000 people died, showing how much good preparation reduces the effects.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q1 B

prompt:
1C. Rocks
Explain the formation of each of the following, with reference to examples that you have studied:
- One sedimentary rock
- One metamorphic rock.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
One sedimentary rock named: 2 marks. One metamorphic rock named: 2 marks. Explanation of formation of sedimentary rock: 6/7 SRPs. Explanation of formation of metamorphic rock: 7/6 SRPs (13 SRPs x 2 marks in total).
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP per rock for a named location linked to the rock.
- Max 1 x SRP per rock if it is only described with no reference to formation - the focus is on formation.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Max 7 x SRPs if only one rock is dealt with. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Sedimentary rock: Limestone (e.g. the Burren, Co. Clare).
Limestone is an organic sedimentary rock. It formed about 300-350 million years ago (the Carboniferous period), when Ireland lay under a warm, clear, shallow tropical sea near the equator. Sea creatures such as corals and shellfish took calcium carbonate from the seawater to build their shells and skeletons. When they died, their remains sank and built up in layers on the sea floor. Over millions of years these layers were buried by more and more sediment. The weight of the layers above squeezed out the water (compaction) and minerals in the water cemented the pieces together (cementation), turning them into solid rock. This is called lithification. Limestone is grey, made of calcium carbonate, and has horizontal bedding planes (where the layers meet) and vertical joints, and fossils can often be seen in it. Later earth movements lifted it above sea level. Limestone covers about half of Ireland, especially the Central Lowlands and the Burren.

Metamorphic rock: Marble (e.g. Connemara, Co. Galway).
Marble is a metamorphic rock formed when limestone is changed by great heat and/or pressure. This happens in two ways. In contact metamorphism, magma pushes up into the crust and its intense heat 'bakes' the limestone around it. In regional metamorphism, huge pressure during plate collisions and mountain building, as during the Caledonian folding about 400 million years ago, changes rock over a wide area. The calcium carbonate in the limestone recrystallises into larger, tightly interlocking crystals. Fossils and bedding planes are destroyed, and the rock becomes harder and can be polished. Pure marble is white; impurities give coloured marble, such as the famous green Connemara marble, coloured by the mineral serpentine. Marble is also found in Carrara, Italy, and is used for buildings and sculptures.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q1 C

model_answer:

(ii) Caves (caverns) and stalactites. (Also stalagmites, pillars/columns, swallow holes, underground rivers.)
(iii) Carbonation.

prompt:
2B. Landscape Development
Answer (i) or (ii)
(i) Examine the role of the processes of erosion on the formation of one fluvial landform or one coastal landform or one glacial landform that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Process of erosion identified: 2 marks. Landform named: 2 marks. Examination: 13 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second process of erosion identified; all further processes must be examined.
- Credit 1 x SRP for an example.
- Focus is on the processes of erosion forming ONE landform. Explaining deposition gets 0 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Max 2 x SRPs for a mere description of the landform with no reference to formation. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Landform: a waterfall, e.g. Torc Waterfall, Co. Kerry, or Niagara Falls on the USA-Canada border.

Waterfalls form in the youthful stage of a river, where the river has lots of energy and is cutting down. They form where a band of hard, resistant rock lies across the river on top of a band of softer rock.

Hydraulic action: the force of the moving water hits the river bed and banks, forcing water and air into cracks and loosening pieces of rock. The softer rock is worn away faster than the hard rock above it (differential erosion). A small step forms in the river bed.

Abrasion: the river picks up stones and boulders and hurls them against the bed and banks, wearing them away. As the water falls over the step, it swirls the stones round and round at the base, drilling out a deep hollow called a plunge pool.

Undercutting: hydraulic action and abrasion in the plunge pool, and spray hitting the back wall, wear away the soft rock under the hard cap rock. This leaves an overhang of hard rock.

Collapse and retreat: in time the overhang becomes too heavy, is no longer supported and collapses into the plunge pool. The fallen rocks are then used as tools for more abrasion. The process repeats, so the waterfall slowly moves upstream. As it retreats it leaves a steep-sided gorge downstream; Niagara Falls retreats about 1 m a year and has cut a gorge 11 km long.

Attrition and solution: the broken rocks knock against each other and become smaller and rounder (attrition) and are carried away, while some rock minerals are dissolved by the water (solution).

So hydraulic action and abrasion, working on rocks of different hardness, are the key erosion processes that form and develop a waterfall.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q2 B (i)

prompt:
2B. Landscape Development
Answer (i) or (ii)
(ii) Describe and explain the factors governing the operation of one mass movement process that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Factors identified: 2 + 2 marks. Mass movement process named: 2 marks. Description/explanation: 12 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further factors must be described/explained.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a specific example.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Max 2 x SRPs for a mere description of mass movement with no reference to the factors governing it. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Mass movement process: a landslide (also accept mudflow, bog burst, soil creep etc.). Example: the Derrybrien landslide, Co. Galway (2003), and the Oso landslide, Washington, USA (2014).

Factor 1: Gradient (slope).
Gravity pulls all loose material downhill. The steeper the slope, the stronger the pull of gravity compared with the friction holding material in place, so movement is faster. Landslides are most common on steep slopes, such as mountainsides and sea cliffs. When rivers or waves undercut the base of a slope, it becomes steeper and unstable. At Oso, the Stillaguamish River had eroded the foot of the hill.

Factor 2: Water.
Water is the most important factor. A little water helps to hold soil together, but heavy or prolonged rain fills the pores between particles, adding weight and acting as a lubricant. It reduces friction, so the material slides. Most landslides happen after long periods of heavy rain. At Oso, weeks of very heavy rain soaked the hillside; about 8 million cubic metres of material slid at up to 60 km/h, killing 43 people.

Factor 3: Human activity.
People can make slopes unstable. Cutting roads into hillsides steepens slopes; deforestation removes roots that bind the soil; building adds weight. At Derrybrien, the construction of a wind farm on blanket bog disturbed and loaded the peat, and about 450,000 tonnes of peat slid downhill, killing fish in Lough Cutra. Mining and quarrying can also trigger slides.

Other factors: the type of material (clay becomes slippery when wet, while loose rock falls easily), vegetation (roots hold the soil together, so bare slopes move more easily) and earthquakes, which shake loose material and can trigger huge landslides.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q2 B (ii)

prompt:
2C. Plate Boundaries
Describe and explain constructive plate boundaries.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Description/explanation: 15 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 3 x SRPs for locational examples.
- Only constructive (divergent) boundaries count: no marks for destructive or neutral boundaries.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
model_answer:
A constructive (divergent) plate boundary is where two plates move apart and new crust is created.

Cause: the plates are moved by convection currents in the mantle. Heat from the core causes magma in the mantle to rise, spread out under the lithosphere and pull the plates apart. As they separate, pressure is released and magma rises into the gap. This is called sea-floor spreading.

Mid-ocean ridges: most constructive boundaries are under the oceans. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the North American and Eurasian plates separate, is the best example. Magma rises, cools and solidifies to form new basalt crust, building a chain of underwater mountains about 16,000 km long. The plates move apart at about 2.5 cm a year, so the Atlantic Ocean is getting wider. The rocks are youngest at the ridge and get older further away, and they show bands of reversed magnetism (palaeomagnetism), which proves sea-floor spreading.

Volcanic islands: in places so much lava erupts that the ridge rises above sea level. Iceland sits on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge (and a hot spot). Its volcanoes, such as Eyjafjallajokull (2010) and the eruptions on the Reykjanes peninsula since 2021, are mostly fissure eruptions of runny, basic lava that flows long distances. Surtsey formed off Iceland in 1963.

Rift valleys: on land, the crust stretches and cracks along parallel faults, and the block between them sinks to form a rift valley. The Thingvellir rift valley in Iceland and the East African Rift Valley are examples. East Africa is slowly splitting apart and may become a new ocean.

Earthquakes at constructive boundaries are frequent but shallow and usually small, because the crust is thin. Geothermal heat is common: Iceland uses it to supply about 90% of its homes with heating.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q2 C

prompt:
3B. Human Interaction with Surface Processes
Human activity impacts on surface processes.
Examine this statement with reference to one of the following:
- The impact of flood control measures on river processes
- The impact of coastal defence measures on coastal processes
- The impact of human activities on mass movement processes.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Impact on process identified: 2 marks. Examination: 14 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second impact identified; all further impacts must be examined.
- Credit 1 x SRP for an example.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Discussion may be positive or negative.
- Max 2 x SRPs for a mere description of human activity with no reference to the impact on surface processes. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Chosen: the impact of flood control measures on river processes. Examples: the Mississippi River, USA, and the River Shannon / Clonmel, Ireland.

Impact 1: Levees and embankments increase the speed and erosive power of the river.
Along the Mississippi, the US Army Corps of Engineers has built over 5,000 km of artificial levees. They keep floodwater in the channel, so the river cannot spill on to its floodplain. Deposition of alluvium on the floodplain stops, so it no longer gets new fertile soil. The confined water flows faster and carries more load, so more sediment is deposited on the river bed, raising it. The levees must then be raised higher. If a levee fails, the flooding is catastrophic, as in New Orleans during Hurricane Katrina in 2005.

Impact 2: Straightening (channelisation) changes erosion and deposition.
The Corps cut through meander necks on the Mississippi, shortening it by about 240 km. A straighter, shorter river has a steeper gradient, so it flows faster, increasing erosion downstream and moving floods more quickly to towns further down. Natural features such as meanders, ox-bow lakes and wetland habitats are lost.

Impact 3: Dams change the load and deposition.
Dams store floodwater in reservoirs. Behind the dam, the river slows and drops its load, so the reservoir silts up. Below the dam the water has little load ('clear water erosion'), so it erodes the bed and banks more. The Mississippi delta is now shrinking because dams upstream trap sediment, and Louisiana loses about 40 km2 of wetland a year. On the Shannon, the Ardnacrusha dam (1929) controls water levels.

Impact 4: Flood walls and relief schemes in Ireland.
The Clonmel flood relief scheme (2012) on the River Suir built demountable flood barriers and walls, protecting hundreds of homes. However, water is pushed downstream faster, so places further down can flood more easily.

Overall, flood controls protect people and property but interfere with the natural processes of erosion, transport and deposition, often moving the problem elsewhere.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q3 B

prompt:
3C. Weathering
Explain the role of temperature in the process of physical/mechanical weathering.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Reference to role of temperature: 2 marks. Explanation: 14 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second reference to the role of temperature; all further references must be explained.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for relevant processes of physical/mechanical weathering named; all further processes must be explained.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram, and 2 x SRPs for extra relevant information on it not already given in the writing. A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Physical (mechanical) weathering is the breakdown of rock into smaller pieces in place, without any change to its chemical make-up. Temperature changes are the main cause. Two processes are freeze-thaw action and exfoliation (onion-skin weathering).

Freeze-thaw action (frost shattering):
This happens where temperatures move above and below 0 degrees C, often several times in a day, as in upland Ireland and mountain areas such as the Alps. During the day, rainwater or snow-melt seeps into cracks and joints in the rock. At night the temperature drops below freezing and the water turns to ice. As water freezes it expands by about 9-10%, putting huge pressure on the sides of the crack. When the temperature rises above 0 degrees C, the ice melts and the water seeps deeper into the widened crack. The process is repeated over and over, widening the crack until pieces of rock break off. On steep slopes the angular fragments fall to the bottom and collect as scree, as on the slopes of Errigal, Co. Donegal, and Croagh Patrick, Co. Mayo. Freeze-thaw is not common in places that are always frozen or always warm; it needs temperatures that swing around freezing point.

Exfoliation (onion weathering):
This happens in hot deserts such as the Sahara, where there is a large daily range of temperature. During the day temperatures can reach over 40 degrees C, and the outer layers of rock heat up and expand. Rock is a poor conductor of heat, so the inner rock stays cooler. At night, with clear skies, temperatures fall close to freezing, and the outer layer cools and contracts. This repeated expansion and contraction sets up stress between the outer layers and the inside of the rock. Eventually the outer layers peel off like the layers of an onion. Dark minerals in rocks like granite absorb more heat than light ones, so the different minerals expand at different rates and the rock crumbles grain by grain (granular disintegration). Exfoliation domes such as Uluru in Australia show the effect.

In both processes, the changing temperature is what produces the stress that breaks the rock apart.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 1 (Physical Environment), Q3 C

prompt:
4B. Primary Economic Activity
Explain any two factors that have influenced the development of one primary economic activity in an Irish region that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Factors identified: 2 + 2 marks. Explanation of factor 1: 7/6 SRPs. Explanation of factor 2: 6/7 SRPs (13 SRPs x 2 marks in total).
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for specific examples of the primary activity.
- Must be an Irish region: no marks for a European or Continental/Sub-Continental region. No link to a named or clearly inferred region = 0 marks.
- Max 1 x SRP per factor for a mere description of the factor with no reference to the development of the primary activity.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a valid labelled sketch map and 1 x SRP for extra information on it.
- Positive and negative interpretations of development are acceptable.
model_answer:
Region: the Southern and Eastern region (the Greater Dublin Area and South-East). Primary activity: agriculture.

Factor 1: Relief and soils.
Most of this region is low-lying, under 200 m, with gentle slopes such as the plains of Co. Meath, Co. Kildare and the south-east (Wexford, Carlow, Kilkenny). Flat land suits the use of big machinery such as combine harvesters, so farms can be run efficiently. The soils are deep, fertile brown earths, formed under deciduous forest, and are well drained. Glacial deposits (boulder clay) left after the Ice Age add to their fertility. This allows intensive tillage: wheat, barley, oats, sugar beet in the past and vegetables. Co. Meath is known for cattle fattening and Co. Wexford for barley, potatoes and soft fruit such as strawberries. Farms are large - often over 50 hectares - and highly productive, with output per hectare much higher than in the West.

Factor 2: Climate.
The south-east is the driest and sunniest part of Ireland. It is in the rain shadow of the western mountains, with about 750-1,000 mm of rain a year, compared with over 1,400 mm in the west. Summer temperatures average 15-16 degrees C, and Rosslare is one of the sunniest places in Ireland, with over 1,600 hours of sunshine a year. Dry, sunny weather in late summer allows cereals to ripen and be harvested. The growing season is long (about 280 days), so grass grows for most of the year, supporting dairy and beef farming. As a result, about 80% of Ireland's cereals are grown in the south and east.

Markets also help: Dublin's population of over 1.4 million, and ports such as Rosslare and Dublin, give farmers a large nearby market for vegetables and dairy produce.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q4 B

prompt:
4C. Complexity of Regions
Changes in boundaries over time can impact on cultural groups.
Examine this statement with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Reference to change in boundaries: 2 marks. Impact on cultural groups identified: 2 marks. Example: 2 marks. Examination: 12 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second example.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a valid labelled sketch map and 1 x SRP for extra information on it.
- Positive or negative interpretation is acceptable. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Example: the partition of Ireland (1921) and Northern Ireland. Second example: the Kurds.

Change in boundary: until 1921 the whole island of Ireland was part of the United Kingdom. After the War of Independence, the Government of Ireland Act (1920) and the Anglo-Irish Treaty (1921), the island was partitioned. Twenty-six counties became the Irish Free State (later the Republic of Ireland), and six north-eastern counties of Ulster became Northern Ireland, which stayed in the UK.

Impact on cultural groups: the border was drawn to give a Protestant, unionist majority in Northern Ireland, but it left a large Catholic, nationalist minority (about one third of the population) inside the new state. Nationalists saw themselves as Irish and wanted a united Ireland, while unionists saw themselves as British. In Northern Ireland, Catholics faced discrimination in jobs, housing and voting (gerrymandering in Derry). The civil rights movement of the late 1960s led to violence and the Troubles (1969-1998), in which over 3,500 people died. Communities became segregated, with 'peace walls' in Belfast separating areas, and separate schools. In the Republic, the small Protestant minority fell in number. The Good Friday Agreement (1998) brought power-sharing and allowed people in Northern Ireland to be Irish, British or both, and the open border helped cross-border links. Brexit (2020) raised fears about the border once again.

Second example: after World War I, the Treaty of Lausanne (1923) divided the lands of the Kurds between Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran. About 30-40 million Kurds became minorities in four countries, with no nation state. In Turkey the Kurdish language was banned for many years, and in Iraq thousands were killed in the Halabja chemical attack (1988). Changing boundaries have therefore created conflict, discrimination and a loss of cultural rights.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q4 C

Account for population distribution throughout a Continental / Sub-Continental region (not in Europe) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:

An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for factors influencing population distribution; all further factors must be examined.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for named locations within the region.

model_answer:
Region: India (the Indian Sub-Continent). India has about 1.4 billion people, but they are very unevenly spread.

Densely populated areas:
Ganges Valley and Delta: the northern plain along the River Ganges is one of the most densely populated places on earth, over 1,000 people per km2 in Bihar and West Bengal. The flat land and deep, fertile alluvial soils, renewed by annual floods, allow intensive rice and wheat growing. The monsoon gives plenty of rain, and irrigation from the river allows two or three crops a year, so the land can support huge numbers of farmers. Large cities grew here, such as Kolkata (about 15 million) at the delta and Delhi.
Coastal lowlands: the narrow coastal plains of the east (Coromandel) and west (Malabar, Kerala) have heavy monsoon rain, fertile soils and fishing. Kerala has over 850 people per km2. Ports and industry attract people to coastal cities such as Mumbai (over 20 million), India's financial centre, and Chennai.
Urban and industrial areas: industry, services and jobs pull migrants from the countryside, e.g. to Bengaluru, India's IT centre ('Silicon Valley of India').

Sparsely populated areas:
The Thar Desert in Rajasthan has very low, unreliable rainfall (under 250 mm a year), high temperatures and poor sandy soils, so farming is very difficult and densities are low, under 100 per km2 in the west.
The Himalayas in the north have steep slopes, thin soils, cold climate and poor access, so few people live there, e.g. Arunachal Pradesh has only about 17 people per km2.
The Deccan Plateau in the interior lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats. It has lower, less reliable rainfall and thinner soils, so it is less densely populated than the coasts, though the black lava soils (regur) support cotton growing in places.

So relief, climate, soils and economic opportunities explain why India's population is concentrated on the plains and coasts and sparse in the deserts and mountains.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q5 B

5C. Secondary Economic Activity
Account for the development of secondary economic activity in a European region (not in Ireland) that you have studied, with reference to any two of the following factors:
- Labour
- Transport
- Raw materials
- Markets.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Examination of factor 1: 8/7 SRPs. Examination of factor 2: 7/8 SRPs (15 SRPs x 2 marks in total).
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for specific examples of secondary economic activity.
- No marks for an Irish or Continental/Sub-Continental region; no link to a named or clearly inferred region = 0 marks.

- Positive or negative interpretation is acceptable.
model_answer:
Region: the Paris Basin (France).

Factor 1: Markets.
The Paris Basin has the largest market in France. The Paris region (Ile-de-France) alone has about 12 million people, almost a fifth of France's population, and they have high incomes and high spending power. Manufacturers locate close to their customers to cut transport costs and respond quickly to fashions. Consumer industries such as food and drink processing, clothing, cosmetics (L'Oreal) and publishing grew up in and around Paris. As the capital, Paris has many government offices and company headquarters, which create demand for high-tech products, printing and electronics. Being at the heart of the EU single market of about 450 million consumers also attracts manufacturers. Car makers such as Renault (Flins) and Peugeot-Citroen (Poissy) built large plants in the region because so many buyers are close by.

Factor 2: Transport.
Paris is the hub of France's transport network. All main motorways (autoroutes) and railway lines radiate from Paris, so goods can be moved easily to and from all parts of France. The TGV high-speed rail links Paris to Lyon, Lille, the Channel Tunnel and Brussels. The River Seine is navigable for large barges from the Channel to Paris, and Le Havre and Rouen at its mouth are major ports. Heavy, bulky raw materials such as oil are brought in cheaply by sea, so oil refineries and petrochemical plants developed along the lower Seine between Le Havre and Rouen. Charles de Gaulle Airport is one of Europe's busiest, ideal for high-value, light goods such as electronics and aerospace parts. Industrial estates and new towns, such as Cergy-Pontoise and Marne-la-Vallee, were built beside motorways and rail lines to attract industry.

These advantages of a huge, wealthy market and an excellent transport system made the Paris Basin France's most important manufacturing region.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q5 C

prompt:
6B. Socio-Economic Regions
Discuss how economic activity in core regions differs from economic activity in peripheral regions, using examples you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Discussion: 15 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for one named core region and 1 x SRP for one named peripheral region.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for examples of economic activity. Any type (primary, secondary, tertiary), one or more activities.
- Max 2 x SRPs for mere description of economic activity in either core or peripheral regions.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a valid labelled sketch map and 1 x SRP for extra relevant information on it (not already given in the writing).
model_answer:
Core region: the Greater Dublin Area (GDA). Peripheral region: the Border, Midland and West (BMW) region / the West of Ireland.

Primary activities:
In the core, farming is commercial and intensive. Flat land, fertile brown earth soils and a drier, sunnier climate allow large farms (over 50 ha) in Meath and Kildare to grow cereals and fatten cattle, with high output per hectare. The large Dublin market buys vegetables and dairy produce. In the West, farms are smaller (often under 30 ha) and fragmented, on poorly drained gley and peaty soils with high rainfall (over 1,400 mm). Farming is mainly extensive cattle and sheep rearing, many farmers are elderly, and many need off-farm jobs to survive. Fishing is important in the periphery, e.g. Killybegs, Co. Donegal, Ireland's largest fishing port.

Secondary activities:
The core attracts most manufacturing and foreign direct investment. Dublin has excellent transport - Dublin Port, Dublin Airport, the M50 and motorways to all regions - and a large, highly educated workforce from universities such as Trinity College and UCD. Companies like Intel in Leixlip employ about 5,000 people. The periphery has a smaller, older workforce and poorer infrastructure, so it attracts less industry. Factories there are often smaller or food processing, e.g. meat plants. Some medical device clusters do exist in Galway (Boston Scientific, Medtronic).

Tertiary activities:
Dublin is Ireland's main service centre, with government departments, the IFSC (financial services), and the European headquarters of tech companies such as Google, Meta and LinkedIn in the 'Silicon Docks'. Over 1 in 4 of Ireland's workers are in Dublin. In the West, services are fewer and rely more on tourism, e.g. the Wild Atlantic Way and Connemara, which is seasonal and lower paid. Many young people migrate from the West to Dublin for jobs.

So economic activity in the core is more intensive, high-value and varied, while the periphery depends more on small-scale primary activity and seasonal tourism.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q6 B

prompt:
6C. Tertiary Economic Activity
Account for the development of one tertiary economic activity in a Continental / Sub-Continental region (not in Europe) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Examination: 15 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for factors influencing the development of a named tertiary activity; all further factors must be examined.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for specific examples of the tertiary activity.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a valid labelled sketch map and 1 x SRP for extra relevant information on it (not already given in the writing).
- Only one tertiary activity is needed (if more, mark each and give the highest).
- No marks for an Irish or European region; no reference to a named or clearly inferred region = 0 marks.
- Max 2 x SRPs for a mere description of the activity with no reference to its development. Positive or negative interpretation accepted.
model_answer:
Region: India. Tertiary activity: tourism.

Physical attractions: India has a huge variety of landscapes. The Himalayas attract trekkers and climbers, and hill stations such as Shimla were developed by the British to escape the summer heat. The beaches of Goa and Kerala, with a warm tropical climate, attract sun holidaymakers, especially in the dry winter season (November to March). Kerala's backwaters are popular for houseboat holidays, and national parks such as Ranthambore attract wildlife tourists hoping to see tigers.

Cultural and historical attractions: India has a long and rich history. The Taj Mahal in Agra receives about 7 million visitors a year, and Delhi and Jaipur in Rajasthan form the popular 'Golden Triangle'. Religious sites such as Varanasi on the River Ganges attract millions of pilgrims. India has over 40 UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Festivals such as Diwali and Holi, and Indian food, music and Bollywood films add to its appeal.

Transport and access: international airports in Delhi and Mumbai and cheap airlines make India easier to reach. Domestic flights, a huge railway network and luxury tourist trains such as the Palace on Wheels have improved access within the country.

Government policy: the 'Incredible India' campaign promotes India abroad, and e-visas introduced since 2014 have made it easier for foreign tourists to visit. Low costs mean India is good value for European and American tourists.

Economic importance: tourism contributes about 5-6% of India's GDP and supports over 40 million jobs, in hotels, transport, guides and crafts. Domestic tourism has grown fast as India's middle class has become wealthier.

Problems have slowed development: poor infrastructure in rural areas, poverty, pollution, safety concerns and the COVID-19 pandemic, when foreign arrivals collapsed. Over-tourism also damages sites such as the Taj Mahal, where air pollution is yellowing the marble.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 2 (Regional Geography), Q6 C

prompt:
7B. Economic Development
Discuss how levels of economic development can change over time with reference to a developed economy that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Developed economy named: 2 marks. Reference to change over time: 2 marks. Discussion: 13 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second reference to change over time; all further references must be discussed.
- Max 2 x SRPs if the discussion does not refer to a named developed economy.
- Max 2 x SRPs if there is no reference to change over time. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Developed economy: Ireland.

1922-1950s: a poor, rural economy. After independence Ireland was one of the poorest countries in Western Europe. Over half of workers were in farming, mostly small, low-output farms, and the economy depended on exporting live cattle to Britain. In the 1930s the government followed protectionism, putting tariffs on imports to build up native industry, but Irish firms were small and inefficient. In the 1950s unemployment was high and about 400,000 people emigrated.

1958-1973: opening up. The First Programme for Economic Expansion (1958), led by T.K. Whitaker and Sean Lemass, removed tariffs and attracted foreign companies with grants and low tax. The IDA set up industrial estates, and free secondary education (1967) improved skills. Living standards rose and emigration slowed.

1973-1990: EU membership and recession. Joining the EEC in 1973 gave farmers CAP payments and access to a huge market, and regional funds paid for roads. But the oil crises and high government borrowing caused a deep recession in the 1980s, with unemployment of 17% and high emigration again.

1995-2007: the Celtic Tiger. Low corporation tax (12.5%), a young English-speaking educated workforce and EU membership attracted American multinationals such as Intel, Dell, Microsoft and Pfizer. GDP grew by up to 10% a year, unemployment fell to about 4%, and Ireland moved from being a net receiver of EU funds to one of the richest countries in the EU. Immigration replaced emigration.

2008-2013: crash. The property bubble burst, banks collapsed and the country needed an EU/IMF bailout (2010). Unemployment rose to about 15% and emigration returned.

2014-today: recovery. Foreign direct investment in tech and pharma (Google, Meta, Apple) and the services sector led recovery. Ireland now has one of the highest GDP per person in the world and ranks near the top of the Human Development Index, though it faces challenges such as a housing crisis and dependence on a few multinationals.

prompt:
7C. Multinational Company
Examine the mobility of modern economic activities with reference to one multinational company that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
MNC named: 2 marks. Examination: 14 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 2 x SRPs for two named locations.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a valid labelled diagram and 1 x SRP for extra information on it.
- No link to a named MNC = 0 marks. Max 2 x SRPs for a mere description of the MNC without examining the mobility of economic activity.
- The MNC need not be Irish based.
model_answer:
Multinational company: Dell Technologies.

Modern economic activities are 'footloose': they are not tied to raw materials, so a multinational company can move its operations around the world to wherever costs are lowest and profits highest.

Dell was founded in Texas, USA, in 1984 by Michael Dell, selling computers directly to customers. To reach the European market it opened a manufacturing plant in Bray, Co. Wicklow, in 1990, and then a large plant in Raheen, Limerick. Ireland was attractive because of its low corporation tax (10%, later 12.5%), IDA grants, a young English-speaking workforce and access to the EU single market. At its peak Dell employed about 4,500 people in Limerick, making it Ireland's biggest exporter.

As the Irish economy boomed, wages and costs rose. In 2009 Dell moved its manufacturing from Limerick to Lodz in Poland, where wages were about a third of Irish wages and EU grants (about €52 million) were available. About 1,900 jobs were lost in Limerick, with knock-on job losses in suppliers. This shows how easily modern industry can relocate.

Later Dell moved much of its manufacturing again, selling the Lodz plant to Foxconn in 2010 and outsourcing production to contract manufacturers in China, Taiwan and Malaysia, where labour is cheaper still and component suppliers are nearby. Global supply chains mean parts are made in one country and assembled in another.

However, Dell kept higher-value activities in Ireland: its European sales, marketing, customer support and finance centre is still in Cherrywood, Dublin, and in Limerick, employing over 2,000 people. Research and design stays in the USA.

This shows the mobility of modern economic activity: MNCs move low-skilled assembly to low-cost countries but keep skilled, high-value jobs in developed countries.

prompt:
8B. Economic Development
Discuss how Gross National Product (GNP) and the Human Development Index (HDI) can be used as a measure of economic development, with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Reference to GNP as a measure: 2 marks. Reference to HDI as a measure: 2 marks. Example: 2 marks. Discussion: 12 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further references to GNP and HDI must be discussed. Credit 1 x SRP for a second example.
- Accept a broad interpretation of development.
- Max 6 x SRPs if only GNP is discussed, and max 6 x SRPs if only HDI is discussed.
- The focus is on how GNP and HDI measure economic development.
model_answer:
Examples: Ireland / Norway (developed) and Niger / Ethiopia (developing).

Gross National Product (GNP):
GNP is the total value of all goods and services produced by a country's people and companies in a year, including income earned abroad, minus income sent out of the country by foreign firms. It is usually given per person (per capita) in US dollars so countries can be compared. A high GNP per person shows a rich, developed economy. For example, Norway's GNI per person is over $90,000, while Ethiopia's is about $1,000 and Niger's under $700. GNP is easy to calculate and compare and shows the wealth of a country.
However, GNP has weaknesses. It is an average, so it hides inequality between rich and poor people and regions. It ignores the informal economy and subsistence farming, which is very important in developing countries. It does not show quality of life, health or education, or damage to the environment. In Ireland, GDP is inflated by multinational profits, so the government uses GNI* (modified GNI) as a better measure; GNP is better than GDP for Ireland because it takes out profits sent home by MNCs.

Human Development Index (HDI):
The UN created the HDI in 1990 to give a broader picture of development. It combines three measures: health (life expectancy at birth), education (mean and expected years of schooling) and standard of living (GNI per person at purchasing power parity). Each country gets a score between 0 and 1. Ireland scores about 0.95, among the top in the world, with a life expectancy of 83 and high levels of education. Niger scores about 0.39, near the bottom, with a life expectancy of about 62 and most adults unable to read.
HDI is a better measure of quality of life, because it shows how wealth is turned into health and education. But it is still an average, and it leaves out things like gender equality, human rights and the environment.

Using both together gives a fuller picture of how developed a country is.

topic_label: EU policy and Irish primary activity
prompt:
8C. European Union Policy
Examine the impact of European Union policy on the development of primary economic activity in Ireland.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Impact on primary activity identified: 2 marks. Examination: 14 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second impact identified and 1 x SRP for a reference to a policy; all further impacts and policies must be examined.
- Max 2 x SRPs without reference to the impact of EU policy on primary activity, and max 2 x SRPs without reference to EU policy.
- Positive and negative viewpoints are accepted.
model_answer:
Policies: the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) and the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP).

Common Agricultural Policy (CAP):
Impact 1 - higher incomes and modernisation: when Ireland joined the EEC in 1973, the CAP guaranteed prices for farm produce and gave farmers access to a market of millions of consumers. Farm incomes rose sharply. Grants helped farmers modernise with new machinery, milking parlours and better land drainage, making farms more efficient and productive.
Impact 2 - overproduction and quotas: guaranteed prices led to 'butter mountains' and 'milk lakes', so milk quotas were brought in (1984) to limit production. When quotas ended in 2015, Irish dairy farmers expanded rapidly, and dairy exports grew, but this increased pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
Impact 3 - direct payments and the environment: since the 2003 reforms, farmers get payments (now the Basic Income Support for Sustainability) not linked to how much they produce, as long as they look after the land. Schemes such as REPS and ACRES pay farmers to protect hedgerows, water and habitats. Many small farmers in the West depend on these payments, which make up most of their income.
Impact 4 - restructuring: the Early Retirement Scheme and young farmer grants encouraged older farmers to pass on land, helping create larger farms, although the number of farms has still fallen.

Common Fisheries Policy (CFP):
The CFP treats EU waters as a common resource. Ireland has about 15% of EU fishing waters but received only about 4-5% of the catch quotas, because other countries such as Spain and France had large fleets fishing here. Quotas and Total Allowable Catches were set to protect fish stocks, but they limited Irish catches. The fleet was decommissioned (boats scrapped) and jobs were lost in fishing ports such as Killybegs and Castletownbere. After Brexit, Ireland lost a further share of its quota. On the positive side, EU funds helped build harbours and fish-processing plants, and stocks such as Celtic Sea herring have recovered.

EU policy has therefore made Irish farming more modern and profitable, but limited Irish fishing.

prompt:
9B. Conflict of Interest
Examine how conflict may arise between the exploitation of natural resources and the need to protect the environment, with reference to example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Example named: 2 marks. Examination: 14 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a second named example.
- Max 7 x SRPs if only one side of the conflict is examined.
- Max 2 x SRPs if there is no reference to conflict. Not tied to Ireland.
model_answer:
Example: peat extraction on Irish raised bogs (e.g. the Bog of Allen). Second example: deforestation in the Amazon rainforest.

The case for exploiting the resource:
Ireland has few fossil fuels, so from the 1940s Bord na Mona cut peat on a large scale from the midland bogs to fuel power stations such as Shannonbridge and Lough Ree, and to make briquettes and garden compost. This gave Ireland its own energy supply, reducing imports of oil and coal. It created thousands of jobs in rural midland areas with few other employers, and towns such as Rochfortbridge and Lanesborough depended on it. Many families also have turbary rights to cut turf for their own fires, a long tradition.

The case for protecting the environment:
Raised bogs took about 10,000 years to form and are a rare habitat; Ireland once had a large share of Europe's raised bogs, but over 90% have been damaged. They are home to rare plants such as sundews and sphagnum moss, and birds such as the curlew. Bogs are huge carbon stores: when peat is drained and burned it releases carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change. Burning peat was one of the most polluting ways to make electricity. Cutting also causes silt to wash into rivers, harming fish.

The conflict:
The EU Habitats Directive required Ireland to protect raised bogs as Special Areas of Conservation (SACs), and a ban on turf cutting on 53 protected bogs from 2011 caused angry protests from turf cutters, who felt their traditional rights were being taken away. Bord na Mona ended commercial peat harvesting in 2020, and power stations closed, causing job losses in the midlands - the 'Just Transition' fund was set up to help. Bogs are now being rewetted to store carbon and restore habitats, and some are used for wind farms and eco-tourism, e.g. Lough Boora Discovery Park.

Second example: in the Amazon, cattle ranchers, soya farmers, loggers and miners clear the forest for profit, providing jobs and exports for Brazil, but this destroys biodiversity, threatens indigenous peoples and releases carbon, causing conflict with environmental groups.

Describe and explain the land-use zones in any city that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:

An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.

model_answer:
City: Dublin.

Zone 1: The Central Business District (CBD).
The CBD is the commercial heart of the city, around O'Connell Street, Grafton Street and Henry Street. It is the most accessible part of the city, as bus routes, the Luas lines and DART converge there, so it attracts most shoppers and workers. Land values are highest here, so only businesses that make large profits can afford it: department stores (Arnotts, Brown Thomas), banks, offices and hotels. Buildings are tall and densely packed to make the most of expensive land. Few people live in the CBD and it has a large daytime but small night-time population. Government buildings, such as Leinster House, are nearby. Modern offices have spread east to the Docklands, where the IFSC and 'Silicon Docks' (Google, Meta) are located.

Zone 2: Residential zones.
Housing makes up the largest area of the city. Close to the centre there are older, high-density terraced houses and flats built in the 19th century for workers, e.g. in the Liberties, and Georgian houses in Merrion Square, many now used as offices. Further out, low-density suburbs were built in the 20th century, such as Tallaght, Blanchardstown and Clondalkin, with semi-detached houses and gardens, as cars and buses allowed people to commute. Wealthier people tend to live in the south-east suburbs, such as Dalkey and Foxrock, near the coast and the mountains. Today, new apartments are being built near Luas and rail lines to increase density.

Zone 3: Industrial zones.
Older industry was located near the port and the River Liffey for transport, e.g. the Guinness brewery at St James's Gate. Modern industry has moved to the edge of the city to industrial estates and business parks, such as Park West and Ballymount, near the M50 motorway, where land is cheaper and there is room to expand and good road access.

Other zones include open space and recreation (Phoenix Park, one of Europe's largest city parks) and transport (Dublin Port and Dublin Airport).

prompt:
10C. Migration
Examine how ethnic and religious issues can arise as a result of migration.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Ethnic issue identified: 2 marks. Religious issue identified: 2 marks. Examination: 13 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further issues identified must be examined.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a named example of where the issues arise.
- Max 2 x SRPs without reference to migration; max 2 x SRPs without reference to religious or ethnic issues.
- Positive or negative interpretation accepted.
model_answer:
Examples: France and Ireland.

Ethnic issues:
Migration brings people of different ethnic groups together. In France, after World War II, millions of migrants came from former colonies in North Africa (Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia) to work in factories. Many were housed in large, poor housing estates (banlieues) on the edges of Paris, Lyon and Marseille. This led to ghettoisation: migrants and their children live apart from the rest of society, with high unemployment (over 20% among young people) and poor services. Discrimination in jobs and housing is common, and people with Arabic names are less likely to be called for interviews. Tensions led to riots in 2005 and again in 2023, after police shootings of young men of North African background. Far-right parties such as the National Rally have gained support by blaming immigrants for crime and unemployment.
In Ireland, immigration grew quickly after 1995, and about 20% of the population is now foreign-born. This has brought a more multicultural society, but also racism, and in recent years protests against International Protection centres and the Dublin riots of November 2023.

Religious issues:
Migration can bring new religions into a country. France is a secular state (laïcité), with a strict separation of religion and state. It has about 5-6 million Muslims, the largest Muslim population in Western Europe. Conflict has arisen over religious dress: a 2004 law banned headscarves and other religious symbols in state schools, and a 2010 law banned face-covering veils (the burqa and niqab) in public. Many Muslims feel this unfairly targets them. Terrorist attacks, such as the Charlie Hebdo shooting (2015) and the Bataclan attacks, increased Islamophobia.
In Ireland, which was mainly Catholic, migration has increased religious diversity - there are now mosques, Orthodox and Pentecostal churches - and it has raised questions about the control of schools, around 90% of which are run by the Catholic Church, leading to calls for more multi-denominational schools such as Educate Together.

Positively, migration brings cultural diversity, festivals and food, and integration programmes and education can reduce these tensions.

prompt:
11B. Population Characteristics
Examine how changing fertility and mortality rates impact on population structure, with reference to an example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Impact of changing fertility rates identified: 2 marks. Impact of changing mortality rates identified: 2 marks. Example: 2 marks. Examination: 12 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further impacts must be examined.
- Credit 1 x SRP for a relevant labelled diagram and 1 x SRP for extra relevant information on it (not already given in the writing). A diagram without labels gets 0 marks.
- Max 2 x SRPs if changing fertility and mortality rates are examined without reference to the impact on population structure.
- Max 6 x SRPs if only fertility or only mortality is examined.
- Max 2 x SRPs if the answer does not deal with 'changing' rates.
model_answer:
Example: Ireland, compared with India.

Falling fertility narrows the base of the population pyramid.
In 1961 Ireland's total fertility rate (TFR) was 3.78 and families often had over four children, so the population pyramid had a wide base. Since the 1970s women have had more access to education and careers, contraception became widely available, and the influence of the Catholic Church declined. Housing and childcare costs have also risen. The average age of first-time mothers is now over 31, and the TFR has fallen to about 1.5, below the replacement level of 2.1. As a result, children aged 0-14 are now only about 18% of the population and the base of the pyramid has narrowed. Ireland's pyramid has moved from expansive to stationary and is becoming constrictive, like Japan's. In future there will be fewer young workers unless immigration continues.

Falling mortality widens the top of the pyramid.
Better healthcare, vaccinations, living standards and diet have lowered death rates and raised Irish life expectancy to about 83. More people survive into old age, so the top of the pyramid becomes wider. In 2022 about 15% of the population were aged 65 or over, and this could reach almost 30% by 2050. Because women live longer than men, there are more women in the oldest age groups. The old-age dependency ratio will rise, increasing the cost of pensions and healthcare and putting pressure on the working population.

India: India's TFR fell from about 6 in the 1950s to about 2.0 today, so the very wide base of its expansive pyramid is slowly narrowing, though about 25% are still under 15. Death rates have fallen and life expectancy has risen to about 70, so the share aged 65+ (about 7%) is growing. India is in Stage 3 of the Demographic Transition Model and is following a similar path to Ireland.

topic_label: Problems in a developing world city
prompt:
11C. Urban Growth - Developing World City
Problems can develop from the growth and expansion of urban centres.
Discuss this statement with reference to one developing world city that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Problems identified: 2 + 2 marks. Developing world city: 2 marks. Discussion: 12 SRPs x 2 marks.
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further problems must be discussed. Any developing world city (or part of one) is accepted.
- Max 2 x SRPs without reference to problems; max 2 x SRPs without reference to the developing world; max 2 x SRPs for discussion of solutions only.
model_answer:
City: Kolkata, India. Kolkata's metropolitan area has grown to about 15 million people, mainly because of rural-to-urban migration from West Bengal, Bihar and Bangladesh, and natural increase.

Problem 1: Shortage of housing and slums.
The city cannot build homes fast enough for the newcomers, so about one third of the population lives in slums called bustees. These are overcrowded, with families living in one-room huts made of mud, wood or corrugated iron. Bustees often lack running water, toilets and electricity, and are built on unsuitable land, such as beside railway lines and canals, which flood in the monsoon. Tens of thousands of people are homeless and sleep on the streets ('pavement dwellers'), especially around Howrah Station.

Problem 2: Poor sanitation, water supply and health.
Much of the sewage system dates from the British colonial era and cannot cope. Raw sewage flows into open drains and the Hooghly River, which is also used for washing and drinking. Diseases such as cholera, typhoid and dysentery spread quickly, especially during monsoon flooding. Rubbish is dumped in huge landfills such as Dhapa, where people pick through waste to earn money.

Problem 3: Traffic congestion and pollution.
Kolkata's streets are among the most congested in the world, with buses, cars, tuk-tuks, trams and hand-pulled rickshaws. Air pollution from old vehicles, coal fires and industry causes respiratory diseases.

Problem 4: Unemployment and the informal economy.
There are not enough formal jobs for the growing population, so many people work in the informal sector as street sellers, rickshaw pullers or rag pickers, with low, irregular pay, no job security and no social protection. Child labour is common.

These problems show that rapid urban growth in developing world cities outpaces the ability of governments to provide housing, services and jobs.

prompt:
12B. Overpopulation
Examine the causes and effects of overpopulation, with reference to an example(s) that you have studied.
(30 marks)
marking_scheme:
Cause identified: 2 marks. Effect identified: 2 marks. Example: 2 marks. Examination of causes: 6 SRPs. Examination of effects: 6 SRPs (12 SRPs x 2 marks in total).
An SRP (significant relevant point) is one piece of correct, relevant information worth 2 marks.
- All further causes and effects must be examined.
- Max 6 x SRPs if only causes, or only effects, are examined.
model_answer:
Example: the Sahel region of Africa (e.g. Niger, Mali, Chad).

Overpopulation happens when there are too many people in an area for the resources and technology available to support them at a decent standard of living.

Causes:
High birth rates: Niger has the highest fertility rate in the world, about 6.7 children per woman. In rural areas children are needed to work on farms and herd animals, and to look after parents in old age as there are no pensions. Many girls marry young (about three quarters before 18), and few women have access to education or contraception. Religious and cultural traditions also favour large families.
Falling death rates: improvements in healthcare, vaccination and clean water since the 1950s have lowered death rates, especially among children, so the population has grown rapidly - Niger's population has grown from about 3 million in 1960 to about 27 million today and could double by 2050.
Limited resources and a harsh environment: the Sahel has low, unreliable rainfall (200-600 mm), frequent droughts and poor soils. Climate change is making droughts more frequent, so the land can support fewer people.

Effects:
Desertification: to feed more people, farmers overcultivate the land, and herders overgraze their cattle and goats. Trees are cut for firewood (deforestation). The soil is left bare and is eroded by wind and rain, so the Sahara spreads southwards.
Famine and malnutrition: when crops fail in droughts, food shortages and famine follow, as in 2005, 2010 and 2012. Millions depend on food aid, and many children are stunted.
Poverty and migration: with too many people for the land, poverty increases, and many young people migrate to cities such as Niamey, causing slums, or try to reach Europe across the Sahara and the Mediterranean.
Conflict: competition for scarce land and water between farmers and herders leads to violence, and armed groups have taken advantage of the instability.

- The explanation must be real explanation, not just more map references.

model_answer:
Reason 1: Coastal location / port.
Map evidence: Dundalk is at the head of Dundalk Bay, with Dundalk Harbour, a Quay and beacons marking the channel at J 06 07 to J 08 08.
Explanation: the sheltered bay and the mouth of the Castletown River gave a safe harbour for ships. The port allowed trade by sea with Britain and Europe, importing coal and goods and exporting farm produce, which encouraged merchants and industry to settle. Fishing also gave food and jobs.

Reason 2: Bridging point / route centre.

Explanation: Dundalk grew at the lowest bridging point of the Castletown River, where routes crossing the river met. A route centre is very accessible, so people from the surrounding area came to the town to trade, attend markets and use services. Today it is on the main Dublin-Belfast corridor (M1 and the railway with a station at J 042 069), so it is easy to reach.

Explanation: the Anglo-Normans built mottes and castles here in the 12th and 13th centuries to control the routeway into Ulster through the Gap of the North. Dundalk was a frontier town at the edge of the Pale, and settlements grew up around the defensive sites, where people felt safe.

13. Views of development and underdevelopment involve contrasting models and approaches to development.
Discuss.
(80 marks)
marking_scheme:
Outline marking scheme (select according to the number of aspects, to the candidate's benefit):
- 3 aspects @ 20 marks each: identifying aspect 4 marks; discussion 8 x SRPs (2 marks each).
- 4 aspects @ 15 marks each: identifying aspect 3 marks; discussion 6 x SRPs (2 marks each).
- Overall Coherence (OC): 20 marks graded - Excellent 20 (excellent ability to relate knowledge to the set question; comprehensive, detailed knowledge); Very Good 17; Good 14; Fair 10; Weak 6; Poor 0 (largely irrelevant answer).
- Allow up to 3 examples to a max of 3 x SRPs (different examples, in different aspects).
- Allow up to 2 labelled illustrations to a max of 2 x SRPs (different illustrations, in different aspects).
- Focus of the question is on the idea that there are different views of development and underdevelopment.
model_answer:
Development is the process of improving people's quality of life. Different groups see development in different ways, and this has produced contrasting models.

Aspect 1: Rostow's Stages of Economic Growth (the modernisation / economic model).
In 1960 W.W. Rostow, an American economist, suggested that all countries pass through five stages of development, as Western countries did. Stage 1 is the traditional society, based on subsistence farming with little technology. Stage 2, preconditions for take-off, sees investment in roads, education and banking, often with outside help. Stage 3, take-off, is when manufacturing grows rapidly, as in Britain during the Industrial Revolution. Stage 4 is the drive to maturity, when industry diversifies and technology spreads. Stage 5 is the age of high mass consumption, as in the USA and Ireland today, where most people work in services and enjoy high incomes. In this view, underdevelopment is just an early stage, and poor countries need investment and trade to 'catch up'. South Korea is often given as an example of a country that followed this path. Critics say the model is Eurocentric: it ignores the fact that Western countries developed partly by exploiting colonies, and it measures development only by economic growth.

Aspect 2: Dependency theory (the core-periphery view).
Writers from Latin America such as Andre Gunder Frank argued that underdevelopment is caused by the way rich countries exploit poor ones. During colonialism, European powers took raw materials from their colonies - cotton from India, rubber from the Congo - and sold manufactured goods back to them. Colonies were kept as suppliers of cheap primary products. Today, many developing countries still depend on exporting one or two raw materials whose prices are set in world markets, e.g. cocoa in Ghana and Cote d'Ivoire. The terms of trade work against them, because manufactured goods rise in price faster than raw materials. Multinational companies take profits back to the core, and debt repayments drain money from poor countries. In this view, the core (USA, EU) develops at the expense of the periphery, so underdevelopment is a result of the global system, not a natural stage.

Aspect 3: Human and sustainable development.
Other views say development is not just about money. The UN's Human Development Index (1990) measures health, education and income. Ireland and Norway score about 0.95, while Niger and South Sudan score under 0.4. The Sustainable Development Goals (2015) aim to end poverty, hunger and inequality by 2030 while protecting the environment, recognising that unlimited growth damages the planet. Development should meet the needs of the present without harming future generations. This view stresses fair trade, gender equality - educating girls lowers birth rates and raises incomes - and local, small-scale projects.

Aspect 4: Self-reliance and aid approaches.
Some leaders rejected Western models. Julius Nyerere in Tanzania tried 'Ujamaa', a self-reliant African socialism based on village co-operatives. Today, NGOs such as Concern and Trocaire support 'bottom-up' development, giving local people the skills and resources to help themselves, e.g. microfinance loans to women. Top-down mega-projects, such as large dams funded by the World Bank, have often displaced people without benefiting the poor.

Conclusion: whether underdevelopment is seen as a stage, a result of exploitation or a lack of human well-being shapes how governments and agencies try to tackle it.
source: 2026 State Exam - Section 4 (Options - Global Interdependence), Q13
